For a few towns no police agency publishes a crime rate for the town alone. There, the rule that nothing shown has more crime than Jamaica could not be tested, and the page says so.
A parking fee counts as published only when the building's own page or a listing states it. A figure from a resident's review is an estimate and is labelled as one.
An apartment with an asterisk has one thing still to confirm: the elevator, whether dogs are allowed, or whether the listing is real and available. The text beside it says what and why.

Some things are worth knowing and never remove an apartment: a floor that is not published, a price quoted for a lease that is not 12 months, a cost that could pass $3,000 once parking and fees are known, a price that already has free months averaged in (only where the listing says so), a special offer (ask what a normal month costs), a condo rented by its owner, a dog weight limit with no number, and a town rule that restricts overnight street parking where the building's parking is not confirmed.
Pet rent is always counted. Where a building does not publish it, the cost uses an estimate, the median of the known pet rents in the same state, and it is marked as an estimate.

Where a building does not publish its parking fee or its required fees, a second figure adds the median of the known ones. It is shown beside the total with utilities and fees and is never used for the $3,000 limit.
Experience and neighborhood figures (medians and ranges) are computed over the apartments shown on the page. A neighborhood's distances from the door are those of its median building.
Where an elevator is named only on a listing site, in its amenity list or its text, it has not been confirmed on the building's own page.
Each apartment carries the date its price was read.
Cost lines that are not published add nothing to the total with utilities and fees. Each receipt names them as not published.

safety.geography: East Orange Police Department: serves East Orange city, population 72,000

parking_rules.summary: Every car parked on an East Orange street overnight (2-6 AM, every day) must have an overnight parking permit, and only on streets signed 'Permit Required to Park'. Streets signed 'NO PARKING 2AM-6AM ANY DAY' allow no overnight parking even with a permit (ticket and tow).
parking_rules.quote: The City of East Orange requires all cars that are parked on the street overnight to purchase and display a parking permit.

parking_rules.summary: Parking Authority wording: a permit is needed 2-6 AM, every day, on all streets that allow overnight parking; residents only.
parking_rules.quote: The City of East Orange requires a parking permit for all streets everyday of the week that allow overnight parking between the hours of 2a.m. to 6a.m.

parking_rules.summary: Overnight street permit: $150 per car per calendar year, pro-rated by month of purchase ($25 if bought in November, $12.50 in December), plus $7.50 transaction fee; $75 senior/disabled. Sold online by the East Orange Parking Authority.
parking_rules.quote: The Overnight Parking Permit Fee is $150 per car for the period of January 1st to December 31st, all permits expire on December 31st.

parking_rules.summary: Renters qualify: documents are driver's license, registration, insurance and proof of residency; if those do not show the East Orange address, a valid lease (or utility/bank statement within 90 days) is accepted. No apartment-building exclusion is stated. An out-of-state license/registration is therefore usable with a lease, per this page.
parking_rules.quote: If the above mandatory documents do not have your East Orange address you must also upload the following documents as proof of residency: a.Valid Lease Agreement

parking_rules.summary: Visitor overnight hang tag: $6 per night, from City Hall licensing / online.
parking_rules.quote: Resident Parking permits can be purchased for $150. Parking hang tag for $6 per night.

parking_rules.summary: Parking Authority lot permits: $55 a month overnight only (8 PM-8 AM) or $80 a month all day, first come first served, valid only in the chosen lot.
parking_rules.quote: Overnight permits between 8pm to 8am are $55 per month or $80 per month for all day parking.

parking_rules.summary: Alternate-side rules apply and must be obeyed even with an overnight permit (the packet says '2am-6pm').
parking_rules.quote: Alternative side parking rules for 2am-6pm must be followed to avoid getting a ticket.

parking_rules.summary: In snow emergencies the emergency no-parking rules and posted NO PARKING signs apply and overnight rules are strictly enforced.
parking_rules.quote: During snow emergencies, all emergency parking rules are in effect. Motorists should adhere to all NO PARKING signs on county and city roads.

dog_rules.summary: Statewide: dogs 7 months or older must be licensed every year through the town where the owner lives, with proof of rabies vaccination. Town fees run $1.50 to $21 per dog, plus $1 state fee and $3 more if not spayed/neutered.
dog_rules.quote: Dogs seven months of age or older must be licensed annually through the municipality where the owner lives.

I have been living here since I can remember, things have changed yet the feeling home is always there. The beauty sunsets and sunrises to the lovely neighbors and street cats.

I appreciate the convenient access to public transportation such as the NJ Transit buses, light rail and the PATH train from Jersey City to New York City, and towards Penn Station, making it comfortable for a resident to explore the location without a car.
The food scene is amazing with cuisines from around the world. The waterfront areas are beautiful and well maintained.
As someone who has lived here for 17+ years it’s been so nice to meet new people, see new things, and just enjoy my surroundings in this area.
voices.context: current resident; says lived there 17+ years

voices.excerpt: I do believe that it is less safe than some other cities but honestly, no where in America is completely safe.
Another major concern is the lack of adequate parking. Finding a parking space is consistently frustrating and inconvenient, especially when returning home after a long day.
That being said, there is obvious growth, and the people are doing their best with what they have. It has a lot of opportunity, beautiful architecture, and nice parks.
But there are select few places that will move you, like views downtown during a sunset. I love the city skyline downtown, I also love the food and cultural diversity.
There were moments when the city felt loud and intimidating, and adjusting to a new environment wasn’t easy.
Similar to NYC, without all the crowdedness and expensive prices.

Being a resident here since I was little, I was able to find a community within my own home, one that provides fun and an abundance of shared laughs whilst also making sure people get the education needed.

For the amount of money residents pay, basic expectations such as a clean, odor-free environment and reasonable parking accommodations should be met. I would not recommend living here based on my experience.
I love my city for how convenient it is everything is 15 minutes to 1 hour away from Major cities like NYC or Philly.
As a young woman, walking around alone often feels unsafe and anxiety-inducing—I almost never do it.
What I really like about Newark is its diversity—you can meet people from all over the world, and that brings a lot of culture, different perspectives, and good food!
It very hectic in the morning times and calm during the night.
I hope that in the future, this problem is solved and my community is much better.

voices.excerpt: I would like to see the parking situation change. Most streets are crowded and if you want to secure a parking spot without paying a fine you have to buy a parking pass.
There are plenty of outdoor spaces, plenty of parks and playgrounds. We have a community YMCA and a community pool.

The vibrant arts scene, especially the Union County Performing Arts Center, always made the downtown feel alive, and the local restaurants offered a mix of flavors that reflected the community’s diversity.
Rahway is a peaceful town, full of color, and kind-hearted people. The citizens of Rahway are very welcoming and accept everyone with open arms.
Rahway is one of those towns that care deeply about the experience of their residents.
The train station in the heart of town made it so easy to connect to New York City, yet Rahway itself had enough character to make you proud to call it home.
Also, the crime rate is not high, the schools are good, and the social life is good. Downtown Rahway has many well-known restaurants and stores.
I like all the restaurants and mini-stores near downtown and I love Rahway River park. I would like to see the parking situation change.

Rahway served its purpose for me: my children were born and raised here; they grew up in the very diverse school system (it's not perfect but if you are involved in your children's education, they will succeed); we commuted easily to the beaches, NYC and all airports.

voices.excerpt: I enjoy that it's safe, convenient and there are a lot of restaurants, stores, and public transportation around.
I'd love to see more parking and clean streets in some parts of Elmhurst, but it's overall pretty decent living in and exploring Elmhurst.
Residents find solace in the green spaces of Elmhurst Park, a serene oasis amidst urban life.

There is a nice selection of restaurants, coffee shops, and local boutiques that give it a welcoming, small-town feel. The people are friendly and community-oriented, and there’s a strong emphasis on family-friendly events and activities.

The place in itself is quite peaceful in majority of the area and lively in others, there’s many stores around that offer a variety of stuff like candy stores, mini markets, corner stores, and generally stores that are budget friendly.
I would like to see a change in the rent stabilization policy
Elmhurst has many opportunities like volunteering and giving back to the community. Elmhurst has a lot of great resources for students and families.
Transportation is easily accessible, with multiple bus stops and train stations.
With many residents it is a bit packed and I overcrowded at times. There are a lot of homeless people and the safety isn't that good.
Elmhurst is a very diverse neighborhood in queens New York. With many residents it is a bit packed and I overcrowded at times.

voices.excerpt: In Bedford-Stuyvesant, I often feel like I have to be more aware of my surroundings because there is frequently police activity and situations that can make the area feel less secure. In contrast, Flushing feels much calmer and safer overall.
Parking is almost nonexistent. The positives of Flushing are the beautiful Kissena Park, and it has a great gym/shopping centers.
However, I do think the area could benefit from improved cleanliness, better traffic management, and more green space.
I appreciate the diversity of the community, the variety of restaurants and shops, and how easy it is to find people from different cultures and backgrounds.
Flushing can be very quiet or a bit noisy depending on the area you're in.
I somewhat live in Flushing since I currently dorm there while attending Queens College, although my permanent home is in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn, where I live with my parents.
It's a little crowded in some parts but overall neighbors know neighbors but you don't feel like you're living in a fishbowl
I live in an area where I have access to a LIRR train station, a bodega, a laundromat, and virtually anything at my fingertips.
I have been living in flushing all my life, and so far it is gradually becoming a not so safe neighborhood.

voices.excerpt: People also smoke CONSTANTLY around here. Parking is almost nonexistent.
We have it all - great food, great parks, great living, great activities.
There is a lot of events and activities, even during the night time. It gets a little crowded sometimes but it's very developed.
I really enjoy how culturally diverse the neighborhood is—there’s always something new to try, from amazing food spots to community festivals.
If there’s one thing I’d like to see improve, it would be the traffic and crowding, especially around Main Street.

voices.excerpt: I like the diversity in cultures, people and how safe the environment is. The train stations are well preserved and there’s less crime going on in the environment.
The parks are not well kept and there is a lot of trash
I feel like nightlife could be a lot better in Jamaica Queens, but the culture is unmatched and it is a melting pot of people like no other.
I would say that Jamaica is an ok place. you're able to leave your house and find something to do. Jamaica ave never gets quiet either.
Hard to find a nice place to rent that isnt super expensive.
I love the neighboor hood although sometimes there may be dangers outside or people from all over the place jamaica is a big family and has a very diverse, connected, and supportive community.
While the city is where most people commute from, it is a bit of a hassle if you travel via Subway as opposed to the LIRR. I will say the transit hub is amazing as you're close to JFK.

voices.excerpt: In Bedford-Stuyvesant, I often feel like I have to be more aware of my surroundings because there is frequently police activity and situations that can make the area feel less secure. In contrast, Flushing feels much calmer and safer overall.
Parking is almost nonexistent. The positives of Flushing are the beautiful Kissena Park, and it has a great gym/shopping centers.
However, I do think the area could benefit from improved cleanliness, better traffic management, and more green space.
There is a wide range of homes, stores, restaurants, and other locations that make this place a good place to live.
Flushing can be very quiet or a bit noisy depending on the area you're in.
It's a little crowded in some parts but overall neighbors know neighbors but you don't feel like you're living in a fishbowl
I live in an area where I have access to a LIRR train station, a bodega, a laundromat, and virtually anything at my fingertips.
I have been living in flushing all my life, and so far it is gradually becoming a not so safe neighborhood.
voices.context: current resident; says grew up / lifelong there

voices.excerpt: People also smoke CONSTANTLY around here. Parking is almost nonexistent.
The environment there allows me to feel more comfortable walking outside, whether it is to get food, spend time outdoors, or simply enjoy the area.
There is a lot of events and activities, even during the night time. It gets a little crowded sometimes but it's very developed.
The neighborhood always feels lively and welcoming. One thing I would like to see improve is less traffic and overcrowding, especially during busy hours.
The best of all worlds - close enough to the city for easy access by subway, bus, LIRR but far enough to feel suburban without being out on the island.

voices.excerpt: I wish there was more diversity, more nightlights for when going home late and also more safety. At night, it’s very scary to walk home alone as a women.
There are also various parks throughout the neighborhood, Bryant park being a well known neighborhood park.

The subway station is situated in an area surrounded by cafe’s, restaurants, grocery stores, hair salons&boutiques.This makes it easy for locals to grab a bite of food or do some quick shopping before/after riding the train.
Great community with a peaceful environment in the DAY.

Buying is pricey — expect $800k+, especially for multifamily properties. It's a solid choice if you're starting out in NYC and great for families looking for space, rental affordability, and local convenience.
How it provides a family-friendly environment as well as a multicultural neighborhood where families of different cultures live.
Another way of transit is the train, Sheepshead Bay is connected to the B and the Q train. These transportation connects to many other lines that allow an easy and smooth transfer.
It feels safe most of the time, it is mostly residential and quiet at night. Diverse residents.
Sheepshead Bay is a diverse, urban neighborhood with strong public schools, is very family-friendly, and has easy access to the beach, Coney Island, and Marine Park for sports and playdates.

Grocery is considered affordable compared to many neighborhoods, there is many fast food chains around the area as well as restaurants for dining. The people are very friendly, though it is not as diverse as other neighborhoods in the upper north.
There is 3 buses and 2 trains that come to Sheapshead bay along with an highway exit. House rents vary from 1,500 to 3,000 It all depends on your preferences and income.
When it comes to transportation, The B and Q trains are the ones that take you to the neighborhood. Some buses that run are the B36, B44, B4, and B49.

voices.excerpt: Yonkers is a moderately safe city depending on which county you're in, but not many crimes or large incidents occur here. My neighborhood is pretty safe and the people are welcoming and friendly.
There’s plenty to do from walking a trail, getting out for a run or bike ride, sitting at the park and looking at the water, and visiting the Utermeyer Garden.
However, I am a female and I have been approached by random men on multiple occasions which has made me feel uncomfortable with going out alone, but there's nothing you can really do about that.
It's normally calm and quiet, with very few disturbances.
I appreciate that Yonkers is a very diverse community where people are generally friendly and welcoming.
There's so much coming to Yonkers, but the true hidden gems are the small local spots that are filled with culture and work ethic.
I would like to see fixes in the roads, fixes in the traffic, and cleaning up the streets in the areas near the library in South Yonkers.
voices.context: current resident; says grew up / lifelong there

voices.excerpt: It has been ranked as a top 10 safest city in the nation. The travel is very easy, whether you have a car or use the public Bee-Line transportation system.

It is a vibrant, hilly patchwork of distinct neighborhoods, each holding its own deep history and tight-knit community feel. My childhood was shaped by the rhythm of the Hudson River views, weekend hangs at Untermyer Park, and grabbing unbeatable food along McLean Avenue.
There is the right balance of entertainment and also quiet in the area.

These challenges have motivated me to pursue higher education and seek ways to contribute back to my community, especially through initiatives that promote educational equity and community development.
The travel is very easy, whether you have a car or use the public Bee-Line transportation system. Something that Yonkers prides itself in is it's growing film industry and the wide diversity.
